CHAPTER XVIII

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten could not sleep all night for anxiety. He was
afraid of thunder and lightning, or he would have made one of the party
that searched Peter's house. As soon as the storm ceased altogether,
he crept downstairs, saddled his mule, and rode to the “Three Kings” at
Sevenbergen. There he found his men sleeping, some on the chairs, some
on the tables, some on the floor. He roused them furiously, and heard
the story of their unsuccessful search, interlarded with praises of
their zeal.

“Fool! to let you go without me,” cried the burgomaster. “My life on't
he was there all the time. Looked ye under the girl's bed?”

“No; there was no room for a man there.”

“How know ye that, if ye looked not?” snarled Ghysbrecht. “Ye should
have looked under her bed, and in it too, and sounded all the panels
with your knives. Come, now, get up, and I shall show ye how to search.”

Dierich Brower got up and shook himself. “If you find him, call me a
horse and no man.”

In a few minutes Peter's house was again surrounded.

The fiery old man left his mule in the hands of Jorian Ketel, and, with
Dierich Brower and the others, entered the house.

The house was empty.

Not a creature to be seen, not even Peter. They went upstairs, and
then suddenly one of the men gave a shout, and pointed through Peter's
window, which was open. The others looked, and there, at some little
distance, walking quietly across the fields with Margaret and Martin,
was the man they sought. Ghysbrecht, with an exulting yell, descended
the stairs and flung himself on his mule; and he and his men set off in
hot pursuit.

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was consumed by a feverish insomnia, his mind trapped in a loop of dread that refused to yield to rest. A superstitious terror held him fast; he feared the very elements that now raged outside—the thunder and lightning—and thus, paralyzed by this irrational awe, he had withheld himself from joining the party scouring Peter's dwelling. Yet, as the storm's fury finally subsided into a trembling silence, the urgency seized him. He crept downstairs, saddled his mule with trembling haste, and galloped to the "Three Kings" inn at Sevenbergen.

There, he found his men slumbering in a chaotic tableau of exhaustion: some sprawled across chairs, others atop tables, and a few curled directly upon the floorboards. Ghysbrecht roused them with furious shouts, demanding answers for their failure. Their responses were a disjointed tapestry of unsuccessful searching, clumsily interwoven with boasts of their own zealousness.

"Fool! To let you go without me!" the burgomaster cried, his voice cracking with indignation. "My life depended on him being there all along. Did you look under the girl's bed?"

"No; there was no room for a man there," one replied dismissively.

"How can you claim such certainty if you did not look?" Ghysbrecht snarled, his patience evaporating like mist before the sun. "You should have looked beneath her mattress, inside the folds of the bedding, and probed every panel with your knives until the wood sang. Come, rise now, and I shall teach you the art of searching."

Dierich Brower rose, shaking the dust from his clothes with a defiant posture. "If you find him, call me a horse and no man."

In moments, Peter's house was once more encircled by the group. Ghysbrecht, the fiery old man, dismounted and entrusted his mule to Jorian Ketel. Clad in determination, he stepped forward alongside Dierich Brower and the others, entering the silent, hollow shell of the home. Inside, nothing stirred. No creature moved, not even Peter himself. They ascended the stairs, the air thick with anticipation, when suddenly one of the men broke the tension with a sharp shout, pointing a finger through the open window of Peter's chamber.

The others turned, their eyes widening as they gazed outward. There, at a modest distance, walking calmly across the golden fields accompanied by Margaret and Martin, stood the fugitive they had hunted. Seizing the moment, Ghysbrecht erupted in an exultant yell. He scrambled down the stairs and threw himself onto his waiting mule. With a unified cry, he and his men spurred their animals, launching themselves into a hot, relentless pursuit.
